content: Colin Carrie, born on April 11, 1962, in Hamilton, Ontario, is a Canadian politician. He currently serves as a member of the Canadian House of Commons, representing the electoral district of Oshawa in Ontario for the Conservative Party of Canada. Carrie was first elected to the House of Commons in June 2004 and was subsequently re-elected in January 2006 and October 2008. On February 7, 2006, Prime Minister Stephen Harper appointed Carrie as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry. Initially, he worked under the Honourable Maxime Bernier and later, starting in August 2007, under the Honourable Jim Prentice. Carrie is the son of a late Royal Canadian Navy officer. During his youth, he lived in several Canadian cities before settling in Oshawa, Ontario, at the age of fifteen. He holds a Bachelor’s Degree in Kinesiology from the University of Waterloo and earned a Doctor of Chiropractic degree in 1989 from the Canadian Memorial Chiropractic College. In his private life, he has worked as a chiropractor and is the co-owner of the Lakeview Chiropractic and Wellness Clinic. He has also served as an executive member of the Durham Chiropractic Society, chaired Spinal Health Week in Durham Region, and acted as the financial secretary of the Oshawa Knights of Columbus. Before the 2004 merger of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada and the Canadian Alliance to form the Conservative Party, Carrie was a director of the Oshawa Progressive Conservative Party Association. In the 2004 federal election, he was elected as the Member of Parliament for Oshawa, defeating New Democratic Party (NDP) candidate Sid Ryan and Liberal candidate Louise Parkes in a closely contested three-way race. He retained his seat in the 2006 election in a tight two-way race against returning NDP challenger Sid Ryan, as part of the first Conservative government elected in Canada in nearly 13 years. During the 38th Parliament, Carrie served as a member of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health. After his election in 2004, he reintroduced Private Member’s Bill C-420, which had previously been introduced by James Lunney. This bill sought to remove the classification of vitamins, minerals, and related products as drugs under the Canadian Food and Drugs Act. The measure, which was endorsed and largely designed by Freedom Party of Ontario activist Trueman Tuck, faced criticism for potentially removing safety provisions in the regulation of natural health products. However, supporters argued that it would benefit small producers in comparison to the pharmaceutical industry. Carrie has also served as Chair of the Conservative Party of Canada’s Automotive Caucus and was a member of the party’s Energy Caucus and Seniors Caucus. On January 19, 2007, Elections Canada charged Alan Clarke, a former activist in Carrie’s 2004 federal election campaign, with alleged defamation against Oshawa NDP candidate Sid Ryan. Ryan, who is the Ontario President of the Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE), also filed a one-million-dollar libel suit against Clarke. Carrie’s campaign manager, Andrew Morin, suggested that the leaflet in question was a result of union disputes over an endorsement by the Canadian Auto Workers and stated that Ryan and Carrie were on good terms. In May 2008, a judge rejected the Crown’s arguments and acquitted Clarke of all charges. On June 3, 2008, General Motors of Canada announced its decision to cease production of light-duty pickup trucks at its Oshawa truck assembly plant in 2009. Carrie, along with Whitby-Oshawa MP and Minister of Finance Jim Flaherty, faced criticism from some members of CAW Local 222 for not visiting a union-initiated illegal blockade of GM’s corporate headquarters in Oshawa, despite many other federal, provincial, and municipal politicians doing so. Carrie was also repeatedly criticized by Local 222 President Chris Buckley, who informed union members that Carrie had failed to make contact until nearly two full days after GM’s announcement.
